title: GenAI on Android & JVM backends
scopeHtml: Scope: Architecture (app -> your backend proxy -> LLM), key safety, Spring AI and LangChain4j, SSE and Kotlin Flow streaming, OkHttp, on-device models (Gemini Nano, MediaPipe), privacy, offline fallback, cost/battery/latency and testing.

notes.title: The big picture - app, your backend, the model
notes.html:
An LLM (large language model) is a program that takes text in and produces text out. You usually do not run it yourself: a provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google) runs it on big GPUs and you call it over HTTPS with a prompt (the text you send). A token is a chunk of text (roughly 3 to 4 English characters) and providers bill per token. The context window is the maximum number of tokens (input plus output) a single call can hold.

On a phone or in a JVM service there are exactly two places the model can live:

  1. In the cloud, called through an API. Powerful, always up to date, costs money per token, needs network.
  2. On the device, a small model bundled with or downloaded to the phone. Free per call, private, works offline, but small and slower to start.

The standard production architecture for cloud models is three hops, never two:

Android app  --HTTPS-->  YOUR backend (proxy)  --HTTPS-->  LLM provider
 (no secrets)            (holds API key, auth,              (Anthropic / OpenAI /
                          limits, logging, prompts)          Gemini)

The middle box is the whole point. It holds the secret key, checks who the user is, enforces quotas, owns the system prompt, logs usage, and can swap the model without shipping a new app.

Real products: Notion AI, Duolingo Max, Grammarly, GitHub Copilot and Spotify's AI features all call their own servers, which then call model providers. The mobile app never speaks to the model vendor directly.

Analogy (after the explanation). A restaurant: the customer (app) tells the waiter (your backend) what they want; the waiter has the key to the kitchen (the LLM) and the till. You never hand customers the kitchen key.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "the app calls OpenAI/Anthropic with Retrofit" as the final design. Interviewers want the proxy and the reasons.
  • Forgetting that the on-device option exists, or presenting it as a replacement. It is a complement (hybrid).
  • Not defining who owns the system prompt: it should live on the server so users cannot edit it.

notes.title: Never ship API keys in the app
notes.html:
An API key is a secret string that proves "this request is from the paying customer". Anyone holding it can spend your money.

Why an app cannot keep a secret:

  • An APK is a zip file. apktool, jadx and strings extract constants in minutes. R8/ProGuard obfuscation renames classes but does not hide string literals.
  • BuildConfig fields, local.properties values injected at build time, strings.xml, even NDK-hidden keys all end up in the shipped binary.
  • Anyone can run a proxy (mitmproxy, Charles) on their own phone and read the header x-api-key from your live traffic.
  • Leaked keys get scraped from GitHub and APKs by bots within hours; the typical incident is a surprise bill of thousands of dollars.

What to do instead:

  • Keep the key only on the server, loaded from an environment variable or secret manager (never committed).
  • The app authenticates the user (Firebase Auth, your own OAuth/JWT login) and sends that token to your proxy.
  • Add Play Integrity API / Firebase App Check so the proxy can reject requests from tampered or non-genuine apps (a signal, not a guarantee).
  • Rate limit per user and set a spending cap on the provider dashboard as a last line of defence.

The proxy call from Python shows the pattern: key from env, never in code.

import os
from anthropic import Anthropic

client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
r = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",  # verify model id in provider docs
    max_tokens=300,
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Say hi"}],
)
print(r.content[0].text)  # prints the model's greeting
// Server side (Kotlin/JVM). The key is read from the environment, never from source code.
val apiKey: String = System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY")
    ?: error("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set") // fail fast at startup
// Android side: there is NO key. Only a user token:
// request.header("Authorization", "Bearer $userJwt")
// Server side (Java). The Anthropic Java SDK can read the env var itself.
// AnthropicClient client = AnthropicOkHttpClient.fromEnv(); // verify in SDK docs
String apiKey = System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY");
if (apiKey == null) throw new IllegalStateException("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set");
// Android never contains this line.

Analogy. Writing your bank PIN on the front of the debit card. Obfuscation is just using a smaller font.

Common interview traps.

  • "I will obfuscate/encrypt the key in the APK." The app must decrypt it to use it, so an attacker can too.
  • "I will restrict the key by package name." Anthropic/OpenAI keys have no such restriction (Google API keys can, but that is not a license to embed LLM keys).
  • Forgetting that user authentication is separate from the API key: the proxy must know which user is asking to rate limit them.

notes.title: A minimal proxy with Spring AI
notes.html:
Spring AI is a Spring project that gives Java/Kotlin backends one API for many model providers (similar idea to what Spring Data does for databases). The central class is ChatClient, a fluent builder for calls. You add a starter dependency for your provider (for Anthropic it is spring-ai-starter-model-anthropic; verify the artifact name for your Spring AI version) and set properties:

spring.ai.anthropic.api-key=${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}
spring.ai.anthropic.chat.options.model=claude-sonnet-5-5
spring.ai.anthropic.chat.options.max-tokens=1024

Request flow in the proxy:

POST /api/chat {question}
  -> authenticate user (JWT)
  -> check quota
  -> build prompt: server-owned system prompt + user question
  -> call model
  -> record tokens used
  -> return answer
# Python equivalent: a FastAPI proxy (the Spring AI idea without Spring).
from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
from anthropic import Anthropic

app = FastAPI()
client = Anthropic()
SYSTEM = "You are a concise support assistant for ShopApp."  # lives on the server

@app.post("/api/chat")
def chat(body: dict, authorization: str = Header(None)):
    if not authorization:                      # replace with real JWT validation
        raise HTTPException(401)
    r = client.messages.create(
        model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500, system=SYSTEM,
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body["question"]}])
    return {"answer": r.content[0].text}       # returns {"answer": "..."}
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
class ChatController(builder: ChatClient.Builder) {
    // Spring AI auto-configures the Builder from application properties.
    private val chat = builder
        .defaultSystem("You are a concise support assistant for ShopApp.")
        .build()

    @PostMapping("/chat")
    fun ask(@RequestBody req: AskRequest): AskResponse =
        AskResponse(chat.prompt().user(req.question).call().content() ?: "")
    // returns the full answer as JSON once the model finishes
}
data class AskRequest(val question: String)
data class AskResponse(val answer: String)
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
class ChatController {
    private final ChatClient chat;

    ChatController(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        this.chat = builder
            .defaultSystem("You are a concise support assistant for ShopApp.")
            .build();
    }

    @PostMapping("/chat")
    Map<String, String> ask(@RequestBody Map<String, String> req) {
        String answer = chat.prompt().user(req.get("question")).call().content();
        return Map.of("answer", answer); // {"answer": "..."}
    }
}

Production notes: set HTTP timeouts (LLM calls can take 10 to 60 s), cap max-tokens server side so a malicious client cannot request huge outputs, and never let the client send the system prompt or the model name.

Analogy. A bank teller window: the customer asks, the teller checks ID, uses the vault, and hands back only the result.

Common interview traps.

  • Accepting model or system from the client request body (cost and prompt-injection risk).
  • Blocking servlet threads on long calls without a timeout or without virtual threads / reactive stack.
  • Returning raw provider errors to the app; map 429/5xx to your own clean error codes.

notes.title: LangChain4j as the alternative JVM toolkit
notes.html:
LangChain4j is a separate, popular JVM library (not part of Spring) that offers model classes, chat memory, retrieval and a neat feature called AI Services: you write a Java interface and the library implements it by calling the model. It works in plain Java, Quarkus, Micronaut or Spring Boot (it has a Spring Boot starter).

Spring AI vs LangChain4j: both abstract providers, both support streaming, tools and RAG. Spring AI fits tightly into Spring conventions (properties, observability, Actuator); LangChain4j is framework-neutral and has strong AI Services ergonomics. Pick the one that matches your stack; interviewers care that you can justify it.

# Python equivalent: raw SDK with a tiny wrapper function (no framework needed).
from anthropic import Anthropic
client = Anthropic()

def support_answer(question: str) -> str:
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=400,
        system="You are a support agent.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}])
    return r.content[0].text

print(support_answer("How do I reset my password?"))  # prints the answer
interface Assistant {
    @dev.langchain4j.service.SystemMessage("You are a support agent.")
    fun answer(question: String): String
}

val model = AnthropicChatModel.builder()
    .apiKey(System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
    .modelName("claude-sonnet-5-5")
    .build()                                   // verify builder options in docs

val assistant = AiServices.create(Assistant::class.java, model)
println(assistant.answer("How do I reset my password?")) // prints the answer
interface Assistant {
    @dev.langchain4j.service.SystemMessage("You are a support agent.")
    String answer(String question);
}

ChatModel model = AnthropicChatModel.builder()
    .apiKey(System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"))
    .modelName("claude-sonnet-5-5")
    .build();                                  // verify class names for your version (1.x)

Assistant assistant = AiServices.create(Assistant.class, model);
System.out.println(assistant.answer("How do I reset my password?")); // prints the answer

Analogy. Retrofit for LLMs: you declare an interface, the library writes the HTTP and JSON plumbing.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing LangChain (Python) and LangChain4j: different projects with similar names and different APIs.
  • Adding a framework when one SDK call would do. A frameworkless call is fine for a single endpoint.
  • Assuming AI Services keep conversation state by themselves; you must configure chat memory per user.

notes.title: Streaming tokens from the server (SSE)
notes.html:
LLMs generate one token at a time. Waiting 15 seconds for a full answer feels broken; showing text as it arrives feels instant. This is streaming. The usual wire format is SSE (Server-Sent Events): a normal HTTP response that stays open, with Content-Type: text/event-stream, where the server writes lines like:

data: Hel

data: lo wor

data: ld

event: done
data: [DONE]

Each blank line ends one event. SSE is one-way (server to client), runs over plain HTTP, and works through proxies; WebSockets are only needed for two-way traffic. Key metric: TTFT (time to first token); streaming does not make total time shorter, it makes the wait feel shorter.

# FastAPI: stream tokens as SSE.
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

@app.post("/api/chat/stream")
def stream(body: dict):
    def gen():
        with client.messages.stream(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body["question"]}]) as s:
            for text in s.text_stream:
                yield f"data: {text}\n\n"      # one SSE event per chunk
        yield "event: done\ndata: [DONE]\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")
// Spring AI: .stream().content() returns a Flux<String> (reactor); needs spring-boot-starter-webflux.
@PostMapping("/chat/stream", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE])
fun stream(@RequestBody req: AskRequest): Flux<String> =
    chat.prompt().user(req.question).stream().content()
// Spring wraps each emitted String as an SSE "data:" event.
@PostMapping(value = "/chat/stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
Flux<String> stream(@RequestBody Map<String, String> req) {
    return chat.prompt().user(req.get("question")).stream().content();
    // each token chunk is sent to the client as one SSE event
}

LangChain4j streams with a handler: a StreamingChatModel (for example AnthropicStreamingChatModel) calls onPartialResponse(String), onCompleteResponse(...) and onError(Throwable) (verify exact names in your version). You bridge those callbacks to an SseEmitter or a Flux/Sink.

Production gotchas:

  • Reverse proxies (nginx, some CDNs, API gateways) buffer responses and kill streaming. Disable buffering (X-Accel-Buffering: no, proxy_buffering off) and watch idle timeouts (many cut at 60 s); send a comment line (: ping) as heartbeat.
  • Mobile networks drop connections. Decide whether a dropped stream is retried from scratch or resumed.
  • If the client disconnects, cancel the upstream model call or you keep paying for tokens nobody reads.

Analogy. A live sports commentary versus waiting for the match report next morning.

Common interview traps.

  • Confusing SSE with WebSockets or with chunked JSON. SSE has a defined text format and EventSource semantics.
  • Forgetting to cancel the upstream call on client disconnect.
  • Believing streaming reduces total latency or cost. It improves perceived latency only.

notes.title: Android networking - OkHttp SSE, Retrofit and Ktor
notes.html:
On Android you have three realistic clients:

  • OkHttp (the engine under Retrofit) with the okhttp-sse artifact: EventSources.createFactory(client).newEventSource(request, listener). The listener gets onOpen, onEvent(eventSource, id, type, data), onClosed, onFailure.
  • Retrofit for the normal non-streaming call (@POST("api/chat")). For streaming you can declare @Streaming and read the ResponseBody source line by line, but OkHttp-SSE is cleaner.
  • Ktor client (Kotlin Multiplatform friendly): client.preparePost(url) { setBody(...) }.execute { resp -> val ch = resp.bodyAsChannel(); ... readUTF8Line() }.

Important setting: the default OkHttp read timeout is 10 seconds between bytes; a model that "thinks" for a while can trip it, so set it higher for the streaming client (for example 60 s), and use a separate OkHttpClient (via newBuilder()) so normal calls keep short timeouts.

# Python client side (for comparison / tests): read SSE with httpx.
import httpx
with httpx.stream("POST", "https://api.example.com/api/chat/stream",
                  json={"question": "hi"}, headers={"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"},
                  timeout=60) as r:
    for line in r.iter_lines():
        if line.startswith("data: "):
            print(line[6:], end="", flush=True)   # prints tokens as they arrive
// Android: OkHttp SSE
val sseClient = okHttp.newBuilder().readTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS).build()
val request = Request.Builder()
    .url("https://api.example.com/api/chat/stream")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer $userJwt")
    .post("""{"question":"hi"}""".toRequestBody("application/json".toMediaType()))
    .build()

val source = EventSources.createFactory(sseClient).newEventSource(request,
    object : EventSourceListener() {
        override fun onEvent(es: EventSource, id: String?, type: String?, data: String) {
            println(data)                       // each token chunk
        }
        override fun onFailure(es: EventSource, t: Throwable?, response: Response?) {
            println("failed: ${t?.message}")
        }
    })
// source.cancel() stops the stream
OkHttpClient sseClient = okHttp.newBuilder().readTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS).build();
Request request = new Request.Builder()
    .url("https://api.example.com/api/chat/stream")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + userJwt)
    .post(RequestBody.create("{\"question\":\"hi\"}", MediaType.parse("application/json")))
    .build();

EventSource source = EventSources.createFactory(sseClient).newEventSource(request,
    new EventSourceListener() {
        @Override public void onEvent(EventSource es, String id, String type, String data) {
            System.out.println(data);           // each token chunk
        }
        @Override public void onFailure(EventSource es, Throwable t, Response r) {
            System.out.println("failed");
        }
    });
// source.cancel();

Analogy. Choosing a vehicle: OkHttp is the engine, Retrofit is the car with a dashboard for ordinary trips, SSE is a conveyor belt delivering items continuously.

Common interview traps.

  • Putting the streaming call on a client with a 10 s read timeout and wondering why long answers die.
  • Using a HttpLoggingInterceptor at BODY level on streams: it buffers the whole response and destroys streaming (and logs user prompts). Use it only for debug builds, and never for the SSE client.
  • Forgetting source.cancel() when the user leaves the screen.

notes.title: Turning streams into Kotlin Flow and UI state
notes.html:
A Flow is Kotlin's asynchronous stream of values. The natural mapping: each SSE event becomes one emission. callbackFlow converts the callback API above into a Flow, and awaitClose runs cleanup when the collector stops (screen closed, coroutine cancelled), which is where you cancel the HTTP call.

SSE event -> callbackFlow emits chunk -> ViewModel accumulates text
          -> StateFlow<UiState> -> Compose recomposes the text
# Python equivalent: an async generator is the "Flow".
async def tokens(question):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=60) as c:
        async with c.stream("POST", URL, json={"question": question}) as r:
            async for line in r.aiter_lines():
                if line.startswith("data: "):
                    yield line[6:]

# async for t in tokens("hi"): print(t, end="")   # prints streamed text
fun chatFlow(question: String): Flow<String> = callbackFlow {
    val es = EventSources.createFactory(sseClient).newEventSource(buildRequest(question),
        object : EventSourceListener() {
            override fun onEvent(e: EventSource, id: String?, type: String?, data: String) {
                if (type == "done") close() else trySend(data)
            }
            override fun onFailure(e: EventSource, t: Throwable?, r: Response?) {
                close(t ?: IOException("stream failed"))
            }
        })
    awaitClose { es.cancel() }                 // runs on collector cancellation
}

class ChatViewModel(private val repo: ChatRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _text = MutableStateFlow("")
    val text: StateFlow<String> = _text
    fun ask(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        _text.value = ""
        repo.chatFlow(q)
            .catch { _text.value += "\n[error: ${it.message}]" }
            .collect { _text.value += it }     // append each chunk
    }
}
// Compose: val t by vm.text.collectAsStateWithLifecycle(); Text(t)
// Java on Android has no Flow; use a callback or RxJava / LiveData.
MutableLiveData<String> text = new MutableLiveData<>("");
// inside onEvent:
//   text.postValue(text.getValue() + data);   // append each chunk from the background thread
// In the Activity: viewModel.text.observe(this, tv::setText);

UI details that matter: update state at most every ~30 to 50 ms (batch chunks) or Compose will recompose per token and jank; render Markdown incrementally; keep the screen scrolled to the bottom only if the user has not scrolled up; survive rotation by keeping state in the ViewModel (configuration change must not restart a paid request). Use collectAsStateWithLifecycle so the stream stops when the app is in the background.

Analogy. A water pipe with a tap: the Flow is the pipe, awaitClose is the plumber closing the valve when the house is empty.

Common interview traps.

  • Collecting in lifecycleScope without lifecycle awareness and leaking the stream in the background.
  • Using callbackFlow without awaitClose (compiler error) or forgetting to cancel the call inside it.
  • Appending to a String in state on every token with no batching: O(n^2) copying and jank on long answers.

notes.title: On-device models with Gemini Nano, ML Kit GenAI and AI Edge
notes.html:
An on-device model runs entirely on the phone's CPU/GPU/NPU. Google's route on Android:

  • Gemini Nano: Google's small model, delivered and updated through AICore, a system service on supported devices (Pixel 8 and newer and some other flagships; check the supported device list).
  • ML Kit GenAI APIs: high-level task APIs on top of Gemini Nano such as summarization, proofreading, rewriting and image description. You do not write prompts; you call a task API (for example Summarizer). Newer releases add a more open Prompt API (verify current availability and artifact names in the ML Kit GenAI docs).
  • Google AI Edge: the broader toolkit (LiteRT, formerly TensorFlow Lite, plus MediaPipe) for running your own models on-device.

Typical flow with ML Kit GenAI: create a client, check feature status (the model may be unavailable, downloadable, downloading or available), trigger the download if needed, then run. Always code the "not available" branch.

checkFeatureStatus()
   UNAVAILABLE  -> fall back to cloud proxy
   DOWNLOADABLE -> download() (shows progress) -> then run
   AVAILABLE    -> run inference locally
# Python has no Gemini Nano. The closest local analogue is running a small model with Ollama.
import ollama  # pip install ollama; local server must be running
r = ollama.chat(model="llama3.2:1b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize: ..."}])
print(r["message"]["content"])  # prints the local model's summary
// ML Kit GenAI summarization (verify class/method names against current docs).
val summarizer = Summarization.getClient(
    SummarizerOptions.builder(context)
        .setInputType(SummarizerOptions.InputType.ARTICLE)
        .setOutputType(SummarizerOptions.OutputType.ONE_BULLET)
        .setLanguage(SummarizerOptions.Language.ENGLISH)
        .build())

suspend fun summarize(text: String): String? {
    val status = summarizer.checkFeatureStatus().await()
    if (status != FeatureStatus.AVAILABLE) return null   // caller falls back to cloud
    val req = SummarizationRequest.builder(text).build()
    return summarizer.runInference(req).await().summary  // on-device summary text
}
// Same API from Java (verify names in docs). Futures instead of suspend.
Summarizer summarizer = Summarization.getClient(options);
summarizer.checkFeatureStatus().addOnSuccessListener(status -> {
    if (status == FeatureStatus.AVAILABLE) {
        summarizer.runInference(SummarizationRequest.builder(text).build())
            .addOnSuccessListener(r -> show(r.getSummary()));
    } else {
        callCloudFallback(text);   // not available on this device
    }
});

Real-world: Pixel Recorder summaries and Gboard smart reply features use on-device Gemini Nano; the point is text never leaves the phone.

Analogy. Having a pocket dictionary versus phoning a librarian: the dictionary is instant and private but small; the librarian knows much more but needs a line and costs money.

Common interview traps.

  • Assuming every Android phone has Gemini Nano. Support is limited by device, OS and region; you must handle UNAVAILABLE.
  • Forgetting the first-use model download (hundreds of MB to a few GB; use Wi-Fi/charging constraints).
  • Confusing ML Kit GenAI (task APIs on Gemini Nano) with the older ML Kit (translation, barcode, etc.) and with AI Edge (bring-your-own-model).

notes.title: MediaPipe LLM Inference and bring-your-own-model
notes.html:
When Gemini Nano is not available or you need a specific open model, MediaPipe LLM Inference API runs open models (Gemma family and others; check the supported list) fully on-device from a model file you ship or download. Model files are large (roughly 0.5 to 4+ GB even when quantized, i.e. stored with fewer bits per weight, like 4-bit integers instead of 16-bit floats, to cut size and memory at some quality cost).

Rules of thumb:

  • Do not bundle the model in the APK; download it after install (Play Asset Delivery, Firebase ML model downloader, or your CDN) with checksum verification.
  • Load once and reuse; creating the engine can take seconds and hundreds of MB of RAM. Close it when done.
  • Run on a background thread; first token can take seconds on mid-range phones, and sustained generation heats the device and drains battery (thermal throttling slows it further).
# Python local-model analogue: llama-cpp-python loading a quantized GGUF file.
from llama_cpp import Llama
llm = Llama(model_path="gemma-2b-it-q4.gguf", n_ctx=2048)
out = llm("Q: What is Kotlin?\nA:", max_tokens=64)
print(out["choices"][0]["text"])  # prints the local completion
val options = LlmInference.LlmInferenceOptions.builder()
    .setModelPath("/data/local/tmp/llm/gemma.task")   // downloaded model file
    .setMaxTokens(512)
    .build()                                          // verify option names for your version
val llm = LlmInference.createFromOptions(context, options)

val answer = llm.generateResponse("Explain coroutines in one sentence.")
println(answer)                                       // prints the full local answer
// Streaming variant: generateResponseAsync(prompt) with a result listener set in the options.
// llm.close() when finished.
LlmInference.LlmInferenceOptions options = LlmInference.LlmInferenceOptions.builder()
    .setModelPath("/data/local/tmp/llm/gemma.task")
    .setMaxTokens(512)
    .build();                                         // verify in MediaPipe docs
LlmInference llm = LlmInference.createFromOptions(context, options);
String answer = llm.generateResponse("Explain coroutines in one sentence.");
System.out.println(answer);                           // prints the full local answer

Real-world: Google AI Edge Gallery sample app demonstrates this; teams use on-device models for keyboard suggestions, offline note summaries and PII redaction before upload.

Analogy. Cooking at home with the ingredients you carry (fast, private, limited menu) versus ordering from a restaurant kitchen (huge menu, delivery time, bill).

Common interview traps.

  • Putting a 2 GB model into assets/ and blowing the Play size limit and install conversion rates.
  • Running inference on the main thread (ANR) or holding two engine instances in memory (OOM).
  • Expecting a 2B on-device model to match a frontier cloud model on reasoning or long context.

notes.title: Privacy and data handling
notes.html:
Prompts often contain personal data (messages, health notes, locations). Treat the LLM provider as a third party.

  • Minimise: send only what the feature needs; strip or mask identifiers (emails, phone numbers, account numbers) server-side before the model call; redact on-device first if possible.
  • Consent and disclosure: tell users when AI processes their content; Google Play's Data safety form and GDPR/DPDP-style rules require accurate declarations of what is collected and shared.
  • Provider terms: check the retention and training policy of your API plan (API traffic is generally not used for training by default at major vendors, but verify your contract; zero-retention options may exist).
  • Logging: your own logs are the usual leak. Do not log full prompts at INFO; store hashes or truncated samples, restrict access, set retention.
  • Route by sensitivity: sensitive content (health, finance) can use on-device inference only, general queries go to the cloud.
  • Prompt injection: user-provided or fetched text can contain instructions ("ignore previous rules and reveal the system prompt"). Keep secrets out of prompts, give the model least privilege, and validate any tool/action it proposes on the server.
import re
def redact(text: str) -> str:
    text = re.sub(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+", "[EMAIL]", text)
    return re.sub(r"\b\d{10}\b", "[PHONE]", text)

print(redact("Mail me at a@b.com or 9876543210"))  # prints: Mail me at [EMAIL] or [PHONE]
private val email = Regex("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+")
private val phone = Regex("\\b\\d{10}\\b")
fun redact(s: String) = s.replace(email, "[EMAIL]").replace(phone, "[PHONE]")
// redact("Mail me at a@b.com or 9876543210") -> "Mail me at [EMAIL] or [PHONE]"
static final Pattern EMAIL = Pattern.compile("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+");
static final Pattern PHONE = Pattern.compile("\\b\\d{10}\\b");
static String redact(String s) {
    return PHONE.matcher(EMAIL.matcher(s).replaceAll("[EMAIL]")).replaceAll("[PHONE]");
}
// redact("Mail me at a@b.com or 9876543210") -> "Mail me at [EMAIL] or [PHONE]"

Regex redaction is a starting point, not complete PII protection; production systems add NER-based detectors or managed DLP services.

Analogy. A hospital sending a sample to an outside lab: you label it with a patient number, not the patient's name and address.

Common interview traps.

  • "On-device is private, so no disclosure needed." You still must disclose any data you collect or sync.
  • Logging full prompts and responses to Crashlytics or analytics.
  • Believing the system prompt is secret; assume users can extract it.

notes.title: Offline fallback and hybrid routing
notes.html:
Phones lose network all the time (lift, train, airplane mode, bad signal). A resilient feature has a ladder:

1. Cloud model (best quality)       -> needs network, quota left
2. On-device model (Gemini Nano)    -> offline, smaller
3. Cached answer / simple rule      -> offline, no model
4. Clear message + retry later      -> always available

Implementation points: check connectivity with ConnectivityManager network callbacks, but treat it as a hint (connected does not mean working); rely on a short timeout (for example 5 to 8 s to first byte) then fall back; mark responses by origin so the UI can say "generated on your device"; queue non-urgent requests with WorkManager (constraints: network connected) to run later; cache previous answers in Room keyed by a hash of the normalised prompt.

def answer(q):
    try:
        return cloud(q, timeout=6)       # step 1
    except Exception:
        return local(q) or "You're offline - try again later."  # steps 2 and 4
suspend fun answer(q: String): Answer =
    runCatching { withTimeout(6_000) { cloud.ask(q) } }
        .map { Answer(it, Source.CLOUD) }
        .getOrElse {
            onDevice.summarize(q)?.let { Answer(it, Source.DEVICE) }
                ?: Answer("You're offline. We'll retry when you're back.", Source.NONE)
        }
Answer answer(String q) {
    try {
        return new Answer(cloud.ask(q, Duration.ofSeconds(6)), Source.CLOUD);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        String local = onDevice.run(q);        // null if unavailable
        return local != null ? new Answer(local, Source.DEVICE)
                             : new Answer("You're offline.", Source.NONE);
    }
}

Real-world: Google Keep and Messages use cloud features with on-device fallbacks; Gboard keeps an on-device model so typing suggestions work in a tunnel.

Analogy. A power cut: main grid, then generator, then candles, then "come back tomorrow".

Common interview traps.

  • Relying only on isConnected. Captive portals and weak signals report connected but time out.
  • Silently switching to a weaker model without telling the user or logging it, then being unable to explain quality differences.
  • Retrying a failed paid request in a tight loop; use exponential backoff with jitter and a cap.

notes.title: Cost, latency and battery trade-offs
notes.html:
Cloud cost is tokens in plus tokens out, priced per million tokens (prices change; verify on the provider page). A rough habit: cost per call = (input tokens x input price) + (output tokens x output price), and output tokens are usually priced several times higher than input.

Levers:

  • Model tiering: use a small cheap model (for example claude-haiku-5-5) for classification, routing and short replies; a bigger one (claude-sonnet-5-5 or claude-opus-5-5) only for hard tasks. Verify model ids in docs.
  • Prompt caching: providers can cache a long repeated prefix (system prompt, documents) at a discount; keep the stable part first.
  • Limit output: server-side max_tokens, ask for concise answers.
  • Trim history: send a summary plus the last few turns instead of the whole chat.
  • Response caching: identical FAQ questions need no model call at all.
  • Per-user quotas: free tier gets N requests a day; track tokens from the response usage field.

Latency components: network round trip, queueing, prefill (reading your prompt; grows with prompt size), then decode (about tens of tokens per second). Streaming hides decode time; shorter prompts cut TTFT.

Battery: the cloud path costs mostly radio time (a streaming connection keeps the modem awake; close it promptly). On-device inference loads CPU/GPU/NPU heavily, produces heat and can drain a noticeable share of battery on long sessions, so reserve it for short tasks and prefer charging/Wi-Fi for model downloads.

def cost_usd(usage, in_price, out_price):          # prices per million tokens
    return (usage.input_tokens * in_price + usage.output_tokens * out_price) / 1_000_000

# r = client.messages.create(...); cost_usd(r.usage, 3.0, 15.0)  # example prices, verify
fun costUsd(inTok: Int, outTok: Int, inPrice: Double, outPrice: Double) =
    (inTok * inPrice + outTok * outPrice) / 1_000_000.0
// costUsd(1200, 300, 3.0, 15.0) -> 0.0081 (example prices only)
static double costUsd(int inTok, int outTok, double inPrice, double outPrice) {
    return (inTok * inPrice + outTok * outPrice) / 1_000_000.0;
}
// costUsd(1200, 300, 3.0, 15.0) -> 0.0081 (example prices only)

Analogy. Taxis versus owning a scooter: taxi (cloud) charges per kilometre and per waiting minute; the scooter (on-device) is free per trip but you carry its weight and fuel.

Common interview traps.

  • Estimating cost by request count instead of tokens.
  • Forgetting that every turn resends the whole conversation, so cost per turn grows with history length.
  • Optimising only cost and ignoring p95 latency and the failure rate of the cheap model.

notes.title: Testing GenAI features
notes.html:
LLM output is non-deterministic, so you split testing into layers and keep model calls out of most tests.

  1. Unit tests with a fake model. Put the LLM behind an interface (ChatGateway). In tests return canned text or canned stream chunks, including errors and slow responses. This covers ViewModel state, Flow collection, retry and fallback logic deterministically.
  2. Contract tests for the proxy. Use MockWebServer (OkHttp) or WireMock to simulate the provider and your own backend: SSE format, 401, 429 with Retry-After, mid-stream disconnects, malformed events.
  3. Prompt/eval tests. A small set of fixed inputs with checks that tolerate wording changes: valid JSON, contains required fields, stays under length, refuses forbidden requests, optionally scored by another model ("LLM as judge"). Run nightly against the real model, not on every commit, and track pass rate over time.
  4. UI tests. Compose tests with a fake repository that emits chunks over time (use TestScope/virtual time). Verify typing indicator, partial text, error and cancel states.
  5. Manual and shadow testing. Dogfood, thumbs up/down feedback, and compare model versions on real (anonymised) traffic before switching.
def test_support_answer_fallback(monkeypatch):
    monkeypatch.setattr("app.cloud", lambda q, timeout: (_ for _ in ()).throw(TimeoutError()))
    assert "offline" in answer("hi").lower()   # passes when the fallback path is used
class FakeGateway(private val chunks: List<String>) : ChatGateway {
    override fun chat(q: String) = flow { chunks.forEach { emit(it); delay(10) } }
}

@Test fun accumulatesChunks() = runTest {
    val vm = ChatViewModel(FakeGateway(listOf("Hel", "lo")))
    vm.ask("hi"); advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals("Hello", vm.text.value)      // passes: chunks were appended
}
MockWebServer server = new MockWebServer();
server.enqueue(new MockResponse()
    .setHeader("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
    .setBody("data: Hel\n\ndata: lo\n\nevent: done\ndata: [DONE]\n\n"));
server.start();
// point the SSE client at server.url("/api/chat/stream") and assert the collected text equals "Hello"

Also test: very long answers, emoji and non-Latin text split across chunk boundaries, rotation during a stream, and process death mid-stream.

Analogy. Testing a cooking robot: first check the buttons and timer with a dummy ingredient (fake), then occasionally taste real dishes against a rubric (evals).

Common interview traps.

  • Calling the real LLM in unit tests: flaky, slow, costs money.
  • Asserting exact output strings from the model.
  • Only testing the happy path; most bugs are cancellation, partial chunks, 429s and offline switches.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Architecture: app -> your backend proxy -> LLM provider. The proxy owns the key, system prompt, model choice, auth checks, quotas and logging.
  • Never ship API keys in an APK; obfuscation does not hide them. Authenticate users, add Play Integrity/App Check, set spending caps.
  • Spring AI (ChatClient, .stream().content() returns a Flux<String>) and LangChain4j (AI Services, streaming handlers) are the two main JVM toolkits; a plain SDK call is fine for simple cases.
  • Stream with SSE for perceived speed; watch proxy buffering, idle timeouts, and cancel upstream calls when the client leaves.
  • On Android use OkHttp SSE (longer read timeout), wrap it with callbackFlow + awaitClose, hold state in a ViewModel StateFlow, batch UI updates.
  • On-device: Gemini Nano via ML Kit GenAI (AICore, check feature status, handle unavailable and downloads) and MediaPipe LLM Inference / AI Edge for your own quantized models; small, private, offline, battery and thermal costly.
  • Privacy: minimise and redact, disclose, check provider retention, do not log prompts, treat the system prompt as extractable, guard against prompt injection.
  • Offline: ladder of cloud -> on-device -> cache -> message, with timeouts and WorkManager for deferred work.
  • Cost: tokens in plus out, tier models, cache prompts and responses, cap output, trim history, track usage.
  • Test with fake gateways, MockWebServer/WireMock, tolerant evals and Compose tests with virtual time; never assert exact LLM text.

questions.subtopic: App to backend proxy to LLM
questions.promptHtml: You are adding an AI chat feature to an Android app. Why not let the app call the LLM provider directly? What does the architecture look like?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It is the first design question for any mobile GenAI feature. It shows whether you think in terms of trust boundaries, cost control and change management.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LLM is a program that turns a text prompt into text, and the provider runs it and bills per token. I would never call it straight from the app. The app talks to my own backend, and the backend talks to the provider. The backend holds the secret key, checks who the user is, enforces quotas, owns the system prompt, logs usage and can switch models without an app release.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Plain-words terms: a prompt is the text you send; a token is a small chunk of text (about 3 to 4 English characters) that the provider bills for; an API key is a secret string that proves "this request is from the paying customer".

Android app  --HTTPS-->  YOUR backend (proxy)  --HTTPS-->  LLM provider
 (user token only)       (key, auth, quota,                  (Anthropic / OpenAI /
                          system prompt, logs)                Gemini)

What the proxy buys you:

  • Secrecy: the key never ships in the APK.
  • Identity and quotas: you know which user asked, so you can rate limit and bill.
  • Prompt ownership: the system prompt lives on the server; users cannot edit it.
  • Agility: swap model or provider, fix a prompt, add caching, all without waiting for users to update the app.
  • Observability: one place to log token usage, latency and errors.

Cost of the extra hop: one more network leg (a few tens of ms) and a service to run. That is tiny compared with 1 to 15 seconds of generation time.

On-device models are a complement, not a replacement: small, private, offline, but far less capable. The proxy is the main path; on-device is the fallback or the privacy path.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
minimal proxy endpoint (server owns key, system prompt, model):

from fastapi import FastAPI, Header, HTTPException
from anthropic import Anthropic

app = FastAPI()
client = Anthropic()  # reads ANTHROPIC_API_KEY from the environment
SYSTEM = "You are a concise support assistant."  # server-owned

@app.post("/api/chat")
def chat(body: dict, authorization: str = Header(None)):
    if not authorization:                       # replace with real JWT validation
        raise HTTPException(401)
    r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500,
        system=SYSTEM, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body["question"]}])
    return {"answer": r.content[0].text}
// Android side: Retrofit interface to YOUR backend. No provider key, only the user's token.
interface ChatApi {
    @POST("api/chat")
    suspend fun chat(@Header("Authorization") bearer: String, @Body req: AskRequest): AskResponse
}
data class AskRequest(val question: String)
data class AskResponse(val answer: String)
// Android side in Java: same Retrofit idea, still no provider key.
interface ChatApi {
    @POST("api/chat")
    Call<Map<String, String>> chat(@Header("Authorization") String bearer,
                                   @Body Map<String, String> req);
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Answering "Retrofit to the provider API" as the final design.
  • Letting the client choose the model or send the system prompt.
  • Presenting on-device models as a full replacement for the cloud.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What does the proxy cost you? → One extra hop and a service to operate; negligible latency versus generation time.
  2. Can the proxy be serverless? → Yes, but mind cold starts and execution time limits on long streaming responses.
  3. Where would you put the quota check? → In the proxy before the model call, using the authenticated user id, backed by a fast store like Redis.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "the app calls my API which calls OpenAI". Senior: lists the responsibilities of the proxy (auth, quota, prompt ownership, model swap, logging), names the cost of the hop, and treats on-device as a hybrid option.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team that shipped direct provider calls needed a forced app update every time they changed a prompt or model; moving to a proxy turned that into a server deploy.

questions.promptHtml: A teammate wants to put the LLM API key in BuildConfig and obfuscate it with R8. Why is that unsafe, and what should you do instead?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Leaked mobile keys are a classic, expensive incident. The question checks that you understand that anything in the client is public.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An APK is just a zip file. Tools like jadx and apktool read string constants in minutes, and R8 renames classes but does not hide string values. Even if I encrypt the key, the app must decrypt it to use it, so an attacker can too. Anyone can also read the header with a proxy tool such as mitmproxy on their own phone. So the key stays on my server, the app sends a user token, and I add Play Integrity or App Check, rate limits and a spending cap.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Rule: any secret that is needed on the device at runtime is not a secret. Paths that all fail:

  • BuildConfig, local.properties injected at build time, strings.xml: all end up in the binary.
  • NDK/C++ hiding: slows an attacker down by an hour, nothing more.
  • Runtime decryption: the key exists in memory, and the decryption code ships with the app.
  • Traffic sniffing: the key is in the x-api-key header of live requests.

The consequences are concrete: bots scrape GitHub and APKs for keys, and a leaked key often produces a bill in the thousands of dollars within hours.

The fix has layers:

  1. Key only on the server, loaded from an environment variable or secret manager.
  2. Authenticate the user (Firebase Auth or your own OAuth/JWT) and send that token to the proxy.
  3. Verify the app with Play Integrity API or Firebase App Check (a signal, not a guarantee).
  4. Per-user rate limits and a hard spending cap on the provider dashboard.
  5. Rotate the key immediately if it ever leaks.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
key from the environment only:

import os
key = os.environ["ANTHROPIC_API_KEY"]  # raises KeyError at startup if missing: fail fast
// Server (Kotlin/JVM): fail fast if the key is missing.
val apiKey: String = System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY") ?: error("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set")
// Android: no key at all, only: request.header("Authorization", "Bearer $userJwt")
String apiKey = System.getenv("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY");
if (apiKey == null) throw new IllegalStateException("ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is not set");
// The Android app never contains this line.

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "R8 will hide it" or "I will split the key into pieces".
  • Claiming package-name restriction protects an LLM key (Anthropic and OpenAI keys have no such feature).
  • Authenticating the app but not the user, so you cannot rate limit per person.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is Play Integrity enough? → No, it only says the app is genuine; still need user auth, quotas and caps.
  2. The key already leaked, now what? → Revoke and rotate at once, check usage logs, move to the proxy, add a spending cap.
  3. What about a short-lived token minted by my server for the client to call the provider? → Possible with some vendors, but you lose prompt ownership and logging; proxy is simpler.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "do not hard-code it, put it in a config file". Senior: explains why every client-side hiding scheme fails, proposes user auth plus attestation plus quotas plus caps, and has a rotation plan.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A startup's key found in a decompiled APK ran up a four-figure bill over a weekend; the fix was a proxy with per-user limits.

questions.promptHtml: Compare running an LLM in the cloud with running one on the device. When would you pick each on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Mobile GenAI is always a trade-off; the interviewer wants a decision framework, not a favourite.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A cloud model runs on the provider's big GPUs and I call it over the network: very capable, always up to date, but it costs per token and needs connectivity. An on-device model runs on the phone: free per call, private, works offline, but small, limited to supported devices and heavy on battery. I use the cloud for hard or long tasks and on-device for short, private or offline tasks, often both with a fallback.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Aspect Cloud (via your proxy) On-device (Gemini Nano, MediaPipe)
Quality Best, frontier models Small model, weaker reasoning, short context
Cost Per token No per-call cost
Latency Network + queue + generation No network, but slow first token on mid-range phones
Privacy Data leaves the phone Data stays on the phone
Offline No Yes
Availability Everyone Only supported devices, model download needed
Battery Radio time CPU/GPU/NPU load, heat

Good fits for on-device: summarising a note, smart reply, proofreading, classification, redacting personal data before upload. Good fits for cloud: long documents, complex reasoning, tool use, anything needing fresh knowledge.

Google's path: Gemini Nano delivered by the AICore system service, exposed through ML Kit GenAI task APIs, and Google AI Edge (LiteRT, MediaPipe) for your own models.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
the decision as a tiny router:

def route(task, sensitive, online):
    if sensitive: return "on_device"
    if not online: return "on_device"
    return "cloud"
fun route(sensitive: Boolean, online: Boolean): Engine = when {
    sensitive -> Engine.ON_DEVICE
    !online -> Engine.ON_DEVICE
    else -> Engine.CLOUD
}
Engine route(boolean sensitive, boolean online) {
    if (sensitive || !online) return Engine.ON_DEVICE;
    return Engine.CLOUD;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming every Android phone has Gemini Nano.
  • Ignoring the first-use model download.
  • Expecting a small on-device model to match a frontier model.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do you know a device supports it? → Check the feature status API; handle UNAVAILABLE by falling back.
  2. Is on-device always cheaper? → Per call yes, but you pay in battery, thermals, app size and engineering effort.
  3. Could you use both in one feature? → Yes: on-device first for speed and privacy, cloud when it is unavailable or the task is too hard.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "on-device is private and offline, cloud is smarter". Senior: gives a routing policy by sensitivity, task size, availability and battery, and plans the fallback and download path.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A notes app summarised short notes on-device and sent long ones to the proxy, cutting provider spend while keeping private notes on the phone.

questions.subtopic: Why stream and what SSE is
questions.promptHtml: What is streaming for LLM responses, what is SSE, and does streaming make the answer arrive faster?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Streaming is expected in any chat UI. The trap is claiming it reduces total latency.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An LLM generates one token at a time, so a long answer can take 10 to 20 seconds. Streaming sends tokens to the user as they are produced instead of waiting for the end. The usual wire format is SSE, Server-Sent Events: a normal HTTP response that stays open with Content-Type: text/event-stream, where the server writes data: lines separated by blank lines. Total time is the same; time to first token, TTFT, drops, so it feels fast.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Wire format:

data: Hel

data: lo wor

event: done
data: [DONE]

A blank line ends one event. SSE is one-way (server to client) over ordinary HTTP, so it passes through most proxies. WebSockets are for two-way traffic and are rarely needed for chat completions. Streaming helps perceived latency and lets the user stop early; it does not reduce total time or cost.

Gotchas: reverse proxies (nginx, some CDNs) buffer responses and kill streaming; idle timeouts (often 60 s) cut quiet streams; mobile connections drop. If the client disconnects, cancel the upstream model call or you keep paying for tokens nobody reads.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
a FastAPI endpoint streaming SSE, and the Spring AI equivalents:

from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

@app.post("/api/chat/stream")
def stream(body: dict):
    def gen():
        with client.messages.stream(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body["question"]}]) as s:
            for text in s.text_stream:
                yield f"data: {text}\n\n"
        yield "event: done\ndata: [DONE]\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")
// Spring AI: .stream().content() is a Flux<String>; needs spring-boot-starter-webflux.
@PostMapping("/chat/stream", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE])
fun stream(@RequestBody req: AskRequest): Flux<String> =
    chat.prompt().user(req.question).stream().content()
@PostMapping(value = "/chat/stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
Flux<String> stream(@RequestBody Map<String, String> req) {
    return chat.prompt().user(req.get("question")).stream().content();
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying streaming lowers total latency or cost.
  • Confusing SSE with WebSockets.
  • Not cancelling the upstream call when the client disconnects.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. SSE or WebSocket? → SSE for one-way token streams; WebSocket only if the client must push mid-stream.
  2. What is TTFT? → Time to first token; mostly queue plus prompt processing, so shorter prompts help.
  3. How do you keep an idle SSE connection alive? → Send periodic comment lines such as : ping.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "streaming shows text as it arrives". Senior: separates TTFT from total time, knows the proxy buffering and idle-timeout failure modes, and handles cancellation.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Streaming worked locally but arrived as one blob in production until the load balancer's response buffering was turned off.

questions.promptHtml: What is Spring AI, and how would you build a minimal chat endpoint with it? What server-side protections does it need?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: For a JVM backend, Spring AI is the default answer. The interviewer checks you can wire it and also harden it.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Spring AI is a Spring project giving Java and Kotlin backends one API over many model providers, a bit like Spring Data does for databases. Its central class is ChatClient, a fluent builder: you add the provider starter, set the key and model in properties, then call chat.prompt().user(question).call().content(). In production I also set HTTP timeouts, cap max-tokens, keep the system prompt server-side, ignore any model sent by the client, and validate the user token.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Properties (names from the Spring AI Anthropic starter; verify for your version):

spring.ai.anthropic.api-key=${ANTHROPIC_API_KEY}
spring.ai.anthropic.chat.options.model=claude-sonnet-5-5
spring.ai.anthropic.chat.options.max-tokens=1024

Request flow: authenticate (JWT) -> check quota -> build prompt (server system prompt + user question) -> call model -> record usage -> return answer.

LLM calls take 10 to 60 seconds, so blocking servlet threads can starve the pool: use timeouts, virtual threads or the reactive stack. Map provider errors (429, 5xx) to your own clean codes instead of leaking raw responses.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Python equivalent without a framework: see the FastAPI proxy in the first question.
r = client.messages.create(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500,
    system="You are a concise support assistant for ShopApp.",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": question}])
print(r.content[0].text)
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
class ChatController(builder: ChatClient.Builder) {
    private val chat = builder
        .defaultSystem("You are a concise support assistant for ShopApp.")
        .build()

    @PostMapping("/chat")
    fun ask(@RequestBody req: AskRequest): AskResponse =
        AskResponse(chat.prompt().user(req.question).call().content() ?: "")
}
data class AskRequest(val question: String)
data class AskResponse(val answer: String)
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api")
class ChatController {
    private final ChatClient chat;
    ChatController(ChatClient.Builder builder) {
        this.chat = builder.defaultSystem("You are a concise support assistant for ShopApp.").build();
    }
    @PostMapping("/chat")
    Map<String, String> ask(@RequestBody Map<String, String> req) {
        return Map.of("answer", chat.prompt().user(req.get("question")).call().content());
    }
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Accepting model or system from the request body.
  • No timeout, so slow calls pile up threads.
  • Returning raw provider errors to the app.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Where does the API key come from? → Environment variable or secret manager, referenced in properties, never committed.
  2. How do you limit abuse? → Per-user quota, a request-size limit, a server-side max-tokens.
  3. How do you stream? → .stream().content() returns a Flux<String> served as text/event-stream.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: gets the endpoint working. Senior: adds auth, quota, token logging, timeouts, error mapping and refuses client-supplied model or system text.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An endpoint accepting max_tokens from the client let one user request 8k-token answers in a loop and burn a day's budget in an hour.

questions.promptHtml: What is LangChain4j, how does it differ from Spring AI, and when would you use neither?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: JVM teams must choose a toolkit. Interviewers want a justified choice and awareness that a plain SDK call is sometimes enough.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: LangChain4j is a framework-neutral JVM library with model classes, chat memory, retrieval and AI Services, where you write an interface and the library implements it by calling the model. Spring AI is the Spring-native option with properties, Actuator and observability integration. Both abstract providers and support streaming, tools and RAG. I pick Spring AI in a Spring shop, LangChain4j for Quarkus, Micronaut or plain Java, and for a single endpoint I may use just the provider SDK.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• LangChain4j is unrelated to Python LangChain apart from the idea and the name; the APIs differ.
  • AI Services give a Retrofit-like feel: annotate an interface method with @SystemMessage and call it like a normal method.
  • Chat state is not automatic: you must configure chat memory per user or conversation, otherwise each call is stateless.
  • Frameworks add dependencies and abstraction; they pay off when you need several providers, memory, tools or RAG, not for one call.

sections.label: Code

• Mixing up LangChain (Python) and LangChain4j.

1. How do you add memory per user? → Configure a chat memory provider keyed by a memory id.

questions.promptHtml: How do you unit test an Android feature that calls an LLM, given that the output is non-deterministic and each call costs money?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Teams often write flaky, costly tests. The interviewer wants a layered strategy.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I put the model behind an interface such as ChatGateway and use a fake in tests that returns canned text or canned stream chunks, including errors and slow responses. That makes ViewModel, Flow and fallback logic deterministic. Real-model checks are a small separate eval set with tolerant assertions, run nightly, never on every commit, and I never assert exact wording.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Layers:

  1. Unit tests with a fake: states, chunk accumulation, cancellation, retry, fallback.
  2. Contract tests with MockWebServer or WireMock: SSE format, 401, 429 with Retry-After, mid-stream disconnects, malformed events.
  3. Eval tests: fixed inputs; checks that survive rewording (valid JSON, required fields, length, refusal of forbidden requests), optionally scored by another model; run against the real model on a schedule.
  4. UI tests with a fake repository emitting chunks over virtual time.
  5. Shadow testing and feedback on real anonymised traffic before switching models.

Also test: very long answers, emoji and non-Latin text split across chunks, rotation during a stream, process death.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def test_support_answer_fallback(monkeypatch):
    def boom(q, timeout): raise TimeoutError()
    monkeypatch.setattr("app.cloud", boom)
    assert "offline" in answer("hi").lower()   # fallback path used
class FakeGateway(private val chunks: List<String>) : ChatGateway {
    override fun chat(q: String) = flow { chunks.forEach { emit(it); delay(10) } }
}

    val vm = ChatViewModel(FakeGateway(listOf("Hel", "lo")))
    vm.ask("hi"); advanceUntilIdle()
    assertEquals("Hello", vm.text.value)
}
MockWebServer server = new MockWebServer();
server.enqueue(new MockResponse()
    .setHeader("Content-Type", "text/event-stream")
    .setBody("data: Hel\n\ndata: lo\n\nevent: done\ndata: [DONE]\n\n"));
server.start();
// point the SSE client at server.url("/api/chat/stream") and assert the collected text is "Hello"

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Calling the real LLM in unit tests.
  • Asserting exact model strings.
  • Testing only the happy path.

1. How do you test a 429? → MockWebServer returns 429 with Retry-After, assert backoff and UI message.
  2. What is an LLM judge? → Another model scoring output against a rubric; useful but itself needs spot checking.
  3. How do you test quality regressions after a prompt change? → Run the eval set before and after, compare pass rates.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
