sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A flaky CI suite that hit the real model failed one run in ten; a fake gateway removed the flakiness and the bill.

questions.contextHtml: Your Android app (200k monthly users) shipped version 3.2 with the Anthropic key in BuildConfig, obfuscated by R8. Monday morning finance flags that the provider bill was $42 on a normal day and is $3,900 for Sunday. The provider dashboard shows 90% of requests with max_tokens=4096 and prompts unrelated to your product (translation, code generation). Your own backend logs show no matching traffic. A teammate says "we only have 200 real users per day on 3.2, it must be a provider billing bug".
questions.promptHtml: Walk through what you do in the first hour and what you change permanently.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames a billing bug, or only rotates the key and ships a new APK with a different obfuscation setting. The new key leaks the same way within days.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the provider dashboard show source IPs or request metadata? Is spend still rising right now? Does the key have any spending cap? Which app versions embed it? Is the key anywhere else (git history, CI logs)?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Revoke the key now and create a new one used only by the server. Set a hard monthly cap on the provider account. The old app version 3.2 will break for AI features, so I show a "please update" message from a kill switch.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) key extracted from the APK and shared or abused (traffic bypassed our backend entirely, which matches the empty backend logs); (b) key committed to git or leaked in CI logs; (c) a real bug in our app looping requests (rejected: our backend shows nothing and prompts are off-topic); (d) provider billing bug (unlikely, usage rows exist).
  4. How I'd verify each: Decompile the 3.2 APK with jadx and search for the key prefix. Search git history and CI logs for the key string. Compare provider request counts with our backend counts. Check the provider's per-key usage export.
  5. Root cause: A client-side secret is a public secret. R8 renames classes but string literals remain, so the key was recoverable in minutes and then scraped or shared.
  6. Fix: Short term: rotated key, cap, kill switch. Long term: move the key behind a proxy, authenticate users, add Play Integrity or App Check, per-user rate limits, server-capped max_tokens, server-owned model and system prompt.
  7. Prevention: CI step that scans built APKs and repos for key patterns (secret scanning), alerts on spend above a daily threshold, a periodic key rotation, and a code-review rule: no provider keys in the client.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not trust better obfuscation or NDK hiding. I would not leave the old key active "until users update". Attestation can reject some legitimate rooted users; I accept that and log it.
// After the fix the app only sends a user token to our proxy.
val req = Request.Builder().url("https://api.example.com/api/chat")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer $userJwt").post(body).build()
# Proxy-side per-user daily quota check (sketch).
def check_quota(user_id: str, tokens_today: int, limit: int = 50_000):
    if tokens_today >= limit:
        raise PermissionError("quota exceeded")
// Server rejects unauthenticated or over-quota calls before spending tokens.
if (jwt == null || usage.tokensToday(userId) >= LIMIT) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(429).build();
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• The CEO asks you to restore AI quickly without a new APK. → Server-side only: nothing the old app does reaches the new key, so I ship a proxy and a forced-update flow; there is no safe shortcut.
  • Can we restrict the key to our app? → Anthropic/OpenAI keys have no package restriction; do not rely on that.
  • How do we detect abuse sooner? → Per-key spend alerts at hourly granularity and anomaly alerts on tokens per user.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a small team learned about their leaked key from a surprise invoice. The post-mortem fix took two days (proxy plus caps); the lesson was that spend alerts are cheaper than cleverness.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suspects billing bug or proposes stronger obfuscation only.
  • Hire: revokes key, caps spend, moves key to a proxy with user auth and quotas.
  • Strong hire: also adds attestation, secret scanning in CI, spend anomaly alerts and a kill switch for old versions.

questions.promptHtml: How do you consume an SSE stream on Android, and which OkHttp setting most often breaks long answers?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests practical Android networking knowledge beyond "use Retrofit".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I use OkHttp with the okhttp-sse artifact: EventSources.createFactory(client).newEventSource(request, listener), where the listener receives onEvent, onClosed and onFailure. The setting that bites is the read timeout, which defaults to 10 seconds between bytes; a model that pauses can trip it. I use a separate client from newBuilder() with a longer read timeout for streaming, keep normal calls on short timeouts, avoid body-level logging on the stream, and call cancel() when the screen is gone.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Retrofit is built on OkHttp and suits normal request/response calls. For streaming, OkHttp-SSE is cleaner than @Streaming plus manual line parsing.
  • Ktor client is the Kotlin Multiplatform option: preparePost(url) { setBody(...) }.execute { resp -> resp.bodyAsChannel() ... } and read lines.
  • HttpLoggingInterceptor at BODY level buffers the whole response and destroys streaming, and it logs user prompts. Use it only in debug builds and never on the SSE client.
  • Mobile networks drop connections: decide whether a failed stream restarts or resumes, and tell the user.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import httpx
with httpx.stream("POST", "https://api.example.com/api/chat/stream",
                  json={"question": "hi"}, headers={"Authorization": "Bearer TOKEN"},
                  timeout=60) as r:
    for line in r.iter_lines():
        if line.startswith("data: "):
            print(line[6:], end="", flush=True)
val sseClient = okHttp.newBuilder().readTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS).build()
val request = Request.Builder()
    .url("https://api.example.com/api/chat/stream")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer $userJwt")
    .post("""{"question":"hi"}""".toRequestBody("application/json".toMediaType()))
    .build()
val source = EventSources.createFactory(sseClient).newEventSource(request,
    object : EventSourceListener() {
        override fun onEvent(es: EventSource, id: String?, type: String?, data: String) { println(data) }
        override fun onFailure(es: EventSource, t: Throwable?, response: Response?) { println("failed") }
    })
// source.cancel() stops the stream
OkHttpClient sseClient = okHttp.newBuilder().readTimeout(60, TimeUnit.SECONDS).build();
Request request = new Request.Builder()
    .url("https://api.example.com/api/chat/stream")
    .header("Authorization", "Bearer " + userJwt)
    .post(RequestBody.create("{\"question\":\"hi\"}", MediaType.parse("application/json")))
    .build();
EventSource source = EventSources.createFactory(sseClient).newEventSource(request,
    new EventSourceListener() {
        @Override public void onEvent(EventSource es, String id, String type, String data) {
            System.out.println(data);
        }
    });

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Streaming through a client with a 10 s read timeout.
  • BODY-level logging interceptor on the stream.
  • Forgetting source.cancel() when leaving the screen.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why a separate client? → newBuilder() shares connection pool and threads but lets me change timeouts only for streaming.
  2. How do you detect completion? → A final event: done or onClosed.
  3. What about call timeout? → Leave the overall call timeout off or large for streams, since it limits the whole call duration.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use Retrofit". Senior: picks OkHttp-SSE, configures timeouts separately, avoids logging bodies, and plans cancellation and reconnect behaviour.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Answers over about 10 seconds of thinking failed on slow models until the read timeout on the stream client was raised.

questions.promptHtml: How do you turn an SSE callback API into a Kotlin Flow, and why is awaitClose essential?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It tests coroutines knowledge applied to a real streaming case, including cancellation and leaks.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A Flow is Kotlin's asynchronous stream of values. I wrap the SSE listener in callbackFlow: onEvent calls trySend(chunk), onFailure closes the channel with the error, and the final done event calls close(). awaitClose { es.cancel() } is mandatory: it runs when the collector stops (screen closed, coroutine cancelled), and that is where I cancel the HTTP call so I stop paying for tokens nobody reads.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
SSE event -> callbackFlow emits chunk -> ViewModel accumulates text
          -> StateFlow<UiState> -> Compose recomposes

callbackFlow requires awaitClose (otherwise it throws at runtime/compile check). Collect with collectAsStateWithLifecycle so the stream stops when the app is in the background, and hold state in a ViewModel so rotation does not restart a paid request. Errors flow through .catch { }.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
async def tokens(question):
    async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=60) as c:
        async with c.stream("POST", URL, json={"question": question}) as r:
            async for line in r.aiter_lines():
                if line.startswith("data: "):
                    yield line[6:]
fun chatFlow(question: String): Flow<String> = callbackFlow {
    val es = EventSources.createFactory(sseClient).newEventSource(buildRequest(question),
        object : EventSourceListener() {
            override fun onEvent(e: EventSource, id: String?, type: String?, data: String) {
                if (type == "done") close() else trySend(data)
            }
            override fun onFailure(e: EventSource, t: Throwable?, r: Response?) {
                close(t ?: IOException("stream failed"))
            }
        })
    awaitClose { es.cancel() }
}
// Java on Android has no Flow; use LiveData or RxJava.
MutableLiveData<String> text = new MutableLiveData<>("");
// in onEvent: text.postValue(text.getValue() + data);
// Activity: viewModel.text.observe(this, tv::setText);

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Omitting awaitClose or forgetting to cancel the call inside it.
  • Collecting without lifecycle awareness and leaking the stream in the background.
  • Using send from a non-suspending callback instead of trySend.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why trySend? → Callbacks are not suspending; trySend is non-blocking and returns a result.
  2. How do you retry? → retryWhen with a backoff, but only for errors before any text was shown.
  3. What if the buffer fills? → Add .buffer() with a policy or conflate updates for the UI.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "wrap it in callbackFlow". Senior: ties cancellation to awaitClose, handles lifecycle and rotation, and chooses a retry policy.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A missing es.cancel() kept completed screens streaming in the background and doubled token spend for chatty users.

questions.promptHtml: How do you call Gemini Nano through ML Kit GenAI, and what states must your code handle?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: On-device code that assumes availability crashes on most real devices. The interviewer checks that you code the unhappy paths.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: ML Kit GenAI offers task APIs, such as summarisation, proofreading and rewriting, on top of Gemini Nano, which Android delivers via the AICore system service on supported devices. The flow is: create a client, check the feature status, download the model if it is downloadable, run inference if available, and fall back to my cloud proxy if it is unavailable. I never assume support.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
checkFeatureStatus()
   UNAVAILABLE  -> fall back to cloud proxy
   DOWNLOADABLE -> download() (show progress) -> then run
   AVAILABLE    -> run inference locally
  • Support depends on device, OS and region; check the supported-device list.
  • The first-use download can be hundreds of MB; prefer Wi-Fi and charging.
  • ML Kit GenAI is different from older ML Kit (translation, barcode) and from AI Edge (bring-your-own-model).
  • Class and method names change; verify in the current ML Kit GenAI docs.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
# Python has no Gemini Nano. Closest analogue: a small local model through Ollama.
import ollama
r = ollama.chat(model="llama3.2:1b", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize: ..."}])
print(r["message"]["content"])
// Verify class/method names against current ML Kit GenAI docs.
val summarizer = Summarization.getClient(
    SummarizerOptions.builder(context)
        .setInputType(SummarizerOptions.InputType.ARTICLE)
        .setOutputType(SummarizerOptions.OutputType.ONE_BULLET)
        .setLanguage(SummarizerOptions.Language.ENGLISH)
        .build())

suspend fun summarize(text: String): String? {
    val status = summarizer.checkFeatureStatus().await()
    if (status != FeatureStatus.AVAILABLE) return null   // caller falls back to cloud
    return summarizer.runInference(SummarizationRequest.builder(text).build()).await().summary
}
Summarizer summarizer = Summarization.getClient(options);   // verify names in docs
summarizer.checkFeatureStatus().addOnSuccessListener(status -> {
    if (status == FeatureStatus.AVAILABLE) {
        summarizer.runInference(SummarizationRequest.builder(text).build())
            .addOnSuccessListener(r -> show(r.getSummary()));
    } else {
        callCloudFallback(text);
    }
});

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming every phone has Gemini Nano.
  • Forgetting the first-use download and its size.
  • Mixing up ML Kit GenAI, old ML Kit and AI Edge.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is AICore? → The system service that manages and updates Gemini Nano on supported devices.
  2. Do you write prompts? → For the task APIs no; a more open prompt-style API exists in newer releases, verify availability.
  3. Where does data go? → It stays on the device for on-device inference.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "call the summariser". Senior: handles every status, downloads under constraints, and measures the share of users with fallbacks.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An app that crashed on devices without AICore learned that 60% of its users could not run the feature at all.

questions.subtopic: Streaming works locally, breaks in production
questions.contextHtml: Your Spring AI endpoint streams answers fine on a developer laptop: first token in 700 ms. After deploying behind nginx and a cloud load balancer, users see a blank screen for 12 to 20 seconds and then the whole answer appears at once. Roughly 8% of long answers (over 60 seconds) end with the app showing "connection lost". The backend logs show the model producing tokens normally and 200 responses.
questions.promptHtml: What is wrong, how do you confirm it, and how do you fix it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Blames the model being slow or the Android client, and adds a spinner. It never checks the intermediary layers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does curl -N directly against the app pod stream? What sits between client and pod (nginx, ingress, CDN, gateway)? What are the idle and read timeouts? Is gzip compression on?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Add X-Accel-Buffering: no to the response and disable proxy buffering for this route so streaming works while I investigate.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) nginx proxy_buffering on holds the response until it completes; (b) a CDN or gateway buffers or compresses the body; (c) idle timeout (often 60 s) on the load balancer cuts quiet streams; (d) HTTP/1.0 or chunked encoding disabled upstream.
  4. How I'd verify each: curl -N -H "Authorization: ..." https://host/api/chat/stream against the pod and then through each layer to see where chunks stop arriving; read nginx config; check load balancer idle timeout; compare response headers.
  5. Root cause: nginx buffered the upstream response; the 8% failures are the load balancer's 60 s idle timeout hitting long gaps between tokens.
  6. Fix: Short term: proxy_buffering off (or the header) for the route. Long term: raise the idle timeout above the longest expected answer, send : ping comment lines every 15 s as a heartbeat, and make the client cancel and retry cleanly.
  7. Prevention: an integration test that streams through the real ingress and asserts the first chunk arrives within 2 s; a dashboard for TTFT (time to first token) measured at the client edge.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not switch to WebSockets just for this; SSE works once buffering is off. Heartbeats add tiny traffic but keep mobile NATs and balancers from dropping the connection.
# FastAPI: headers that tell proxies not to buffer, plus a heartbeat in the generator.
headers = {"Cache-Control": "no-cache", "X-Accel-Buffering": "no"}
# yield ": ping\n\n" every ~15 s while waiting for the model
@GetMapping("/chat/stream", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE])
fun stream(response: HttpServletResponse): Flux<String> {
    response.setHeader("X-Accel-Buffering", "no")
    return chat.prompt().user("...").stream().content()
}
@GetMapping(value = "/chat/stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
Flux<String> stream(HttpServletResponse response) {
    response.setHeader("X-Accel-Buffering", "no");
    return chat.prompt().user("...").stream().content();
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• It still buffers behind the CDN. → Use a CDN route that disables caching and response buffering for the path, or bypass the CDN for the API host.
  • Corporate proxies on user networks buffer too. → Fall back to non-streaming for those clients when no early chunk arrives.
  • Does compression matter? → Yes; gzip can buffer small chunks, so disable it for text/event-stream.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team spent a day profiling the model before a one-line nginx directive fixed it; the lesson was to test through the real network path early.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames the model or adds a spinner.
  • Hire: identifies proxy buffering and idle timeouts, verifies with curl -N.
  • Strong hire: adds heartbeats, an ingress streaming test and TTFT monitoring, and compares alternatives.

questions.promptHtml: Users type personal information into your AI feature. How do you handle privacy end to end on Android and the backend?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Privacy mistakes become legal and trust incidents. Seniors are expected to design minimisation, consent and logging controls, not just encryption.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: I treat the model provider as a third party. I send only what the feature needs, mask identifiers like emails and phone numbers before the model call, tell users that AI processes their content, check the provider's retention and training terms, and avoid logging full prompts. For very sensitive content I use on-device inference only. Regex redaction is only a first step; production adds NER or a DLP service.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• Minimise: strip fields the model does not need.
  • Consent and disclosure: Play Data safety form and rules like GDPR or DPDP require accurate declarations.
  • Provider terms: API traffic is generally not used for training by default at major vendors, but verify your contract and retention options.
  • Logging: your own logs are the usual leak (Crashlytics, analytics, APM). Log hashes or truncated samples, restrict access, set retention.
  • Route by sensitivity: health and finance on-device, general queries to the cloud.
  • Prompt injection: user or fetched text can contain instructions ("ignore previous rules"). Keep secrets out of prompts, give the model least privilege, validate any action it proposes on the server. Assume the system prompt can be extracted.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import re
def redact(text: str) -> str:
    text = re.sub(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+", "[EMAIL]", text)
    return re.sub(r"\b\d{10}\b", "[PHONE]", text)
print(redact("Mail me at a@b.com or 9876543210"))  # Mail me at [EMAIL] or [PHONE]
private val email = Regex("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+")
private val phone = Regex("\\b\\d{10}\\b")
fun redact(s: String) = s.replace(email, "[EMAIL]").replace(phone, "[PHONE]")
static final Pattern EMAIL = Pattern.compile("[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+\\.[\\w.]+");
static final Pattern PHONE = Pattern.compile("\\b\\d{10}\\b");
static String redact(String s) {
    return PHONE.matcher(EMAIL.matcher(s).replaceAll("[EMAIL]")).replaceAll("[PHONE]");
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "On-device is private, so no disclosure needed."
  • Logging full prompts and responses to Crashlytics.
  • Believing the system prompt is secret.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does redaction break the answer? → Sometimes; use stable placeholders and re-insert values client-side if needed.
  2. How long do you keep logs? → As short as debugging needs; document it.
  3. What about user deletion requests? → Delete stored conversations and any derived data, and confirm provider retention.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use HTTPS". Senior: describes minimisation, redaction limits, consent, retention, logging hygiene and sensitivity-based routing.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Full prompts in a crash reporting tool exposed users' messages to a wide engineering audience; they moved to hashed samples with short retention.

questions.contextHtml: Your commuter app summarises articles with a cloud model. Support tickets say the feature "spins forever" in metro tunnels. Telemetry: 14% of requests happen with a captive-portal or weak connection; the cloud call takes 25 s before the OkHttp call timeout fires; the app checks isConnected before calling and reports it as true. About 40% of your users own devices where Gemini Nano is available. Budget: no more spend on the cloud.
questions.promptHtml: Design the offline and fallback behaviour.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Check isConnected and show an offline banner." Connected does not mean working, and nothing is offered to the user.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Must the summary be available instantly, or can it be deferred? How long can the user wait? Is the text sensitive? What quality drop is acceptable on-device?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cut the first-byte timeout to about 6 s and show a clear error with a retry instead of spinning for 25 s.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) isConnected is misleading under captive portals and weak signal; (b) timeouts are too long; (c) no alternative path; (d) retries without backoff add load.
  4. How I'd verify each: Reproduce in airplane mode, throttled network (Android emulator network profiles) and a captive portal; measure time-to-error.
  5. Root cause: One path, long timeout, trust in a connectivity hint.
  6. Fix: A ladder: cloud (6 s first-byte timeout) -> on-device Gemini Nano if the feature status is AVAILABLE -> cached previous summary from Room keyed by a hash of the normalised text -> a clear message, with a WorkManager job (network-connected constraint) to produce it later. Mark the origin so the UI can say "generated on your device".
  7. Prevention: Track fallback rates by reason, run a nightly check of the on-device path, and test with the network profiles in CI-lite UI tests.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not silently switch models without telling the user or logging the source; quality differs. I would not retry in a tight loop; use exponential backoff with jitter and a cap.
def answer(q):
    try:
        return cloud(q, timeout=6)
    except Exception:
        return local(q) or "You're offline - try again later."
suspend fun answer(q: String): Answer =
    runCatching { withTimeout(6_000) { cloud.ask(q) } }
        .map { Answer(it, Source.CLOUD) }
        .getOrElse {
            onDevice.summarize(q)?.let { Answer(it, Source.DEVICE) }
                ?: Answer("You're offline. We'll retry when you're back.", Source.NONE)
        }
Answer answer(String q) {
    try {
        return new Answer(cloud.ask(q, Duration.ofSeconds(6)), Source.CLOUD);
    } catch (Exception e) {
        String local = onDevice.run(q);        // null if unavailable
        return local != null ? new Answer(local, Source.DEVICE)
                             : new Answer("You're offline.", Source.NONE);
    }
}

sections.html:
• Only 40% have Gemini Nano; what about the rest? → Cache, deferred WorkManager job and a clear message; consider a small downloadable MediaPipe model if the size is acceptable.
  • Users complain summaries differ by device. → Show the source label and keep prompts identical; accept the quality gap.
  • Cost cap? → On-device and cache both cut cloud spend; cache identical articles server-side too.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team replaced a connectivity check with a short first-byte timeout and cut "spinning forever" tickets by most of the volume in a week.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: relies on isConnected only.
  • Hire: timeout plus on-device fallback plus clear UX.
  • Strong hire: full ladder with cache and WorkManager, origin labelling, backoff with jitter and fallback metrics.

questions.promptHtml: How do you estimate and reduce the cloud cost of a chat feature, and why does cost per turn grow during a conversation?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cost surprises kill AI features. The interviewer wants token-based thinking, not request counting.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Cost per call is input tokens times the input price plus output tokens times the output price, both per million tokens, and output is usually priced several times higher. A chat resends the whole history every turn, so input grows with each turn. To cut cost I tier models (a cheap one for simple tasks), cache a long repeated prefix, cap max_tokens server-side, trim or summarise history, cache FAQ responses and track the usage field per user.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Example with illustrative prices of 3 per million input and 15 per million output: a call with 1,200 input tokens and 300 output tokens costs (1200 x 3 + 300 x 15) / 1,000,000 = 0.0081. Prices change, so verify on the provider page.

If each turn adds about 400 tokens to history, turn 10 sends about 4,000 input tokens before your question, so the cumulative cost across a 10-turn chat is roughly the sum of an arithmetic series, not 10 times one turn.

Latency parts: network round trip, queueing, prefill (reading the prompt; grows with prompt size), then decode (tens of tokens per second). Streaming hides decode time; shorter prompts lower TTFT.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
def cost_usd(usage, in_price, out_price):          # prices per million tokens
    return (usage.input_tokens * in_price + usage.output_tokens * out_price) / 1_000_000
# r = client.messages.create(...); cost_usd(r.usage, 3.0, 15.0)   # example prices, verify
fun costUsd(inTok: Int, outTok: Int, inPrice: Double, outPrice: Double) =
    (inTok * inPrice + outTok * outPrice) / 1_000_000.0
// costUsd(1200, 300, 3.0, 15.0) -> 0.0081 (example prices only)
static double costUsd(int inTok, int outTok, double inPrice, double outPrice) {
    return (inTok * inPrice + outTok * outPrice) / 1_000_000.0;
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Estimating by request count instead of tokens.
  • Forgetting history resend.
  • Optimising cost and ignoring p95 latency and failure rate of the cheap model.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What is prompt caching? → The provider stores a repeated prefix and bills it at a discount; keep the stable part first.
  2. Where do you get token counts? → The response usage field, not your own estimate.
  3. How do you stop one user burning budget? → Per-user daily token quotas in the proxy.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "use a cheaper model". Senior: does the token arithmetic, models history growth, and combines tiering, caching, trimming and quotas.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Average cost per active user doubled after launch because chats got longer; trimming history to a summary plus 4 turns cut it by a third.

questions.contextHtml:
Users report that during long answers (about 1,500 tokens) the chat screen janks and the phone gets warm. Rotating the phone mid-answer restarts the request and the user sees the answer start over; the provider bills for both. Profiling shows thousands of recompositions per answer. The relevant code:

class ChatViewModel(private val repo: ChatRepo) : ViewModel() {
    var text by mutableStateOf("")
    fun ask(q: String) {
        text = ""
        CoroutineScope(Dispatchers.Main).launch {
            repo.chatFlow(q).collect { text = text + it }
        }
    }
}
@Composable fun Screen(vm: ChatViewModel = ChatViewModel(repo)) { Text(vm.text) }
questions.promptHtml: Find the bugs and fix them.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Says "use a background thread" and misses the lifecycle and scope problems.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the repo cancel the HTTP call when the collector stops? Which Compose and lifecycle libraries are used? What is the chunk rate?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Stop restarting on rotation and batch updates.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) the ViewModel is created inside the composable's default argument, so rotation creates a new one and re-asks; (b) CoroutineScope(...) is an unmanaged scope, never cancelled, so the stream leaks; (c) one state write per token (hundreds of recompositions per second) and string concatenation copying a growing string, O(n squared) overall; (d) no error handling.
  4. How I'd verify each: Layout Inspector recomposition counts; log ViewModel creation; LeakCanary; count chunks per second.
  5. Root cause: Wrong ViewModel ownership, wrong coroutine scope, and per-token UI updates.
  6. Fix: Obtain the ViewModel with viewModel(), use viewModelScope, collect with a batching step (for example chunked-style time window or sample(40) on an accumulated flow), expose StateFlow, read it with collectAsStateWithLifecycle, and handle errors with .catch. Make repo.chatFlow use awaitClose { es.cancel() }.
  7. Prevention: Compose tests with virtual time; a lint rule against creating scopes manually; a recomposition budget in profiling.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not drop chunks (text must stay complete); I batch, not discard. Larger batches look choppier; 30 to 50 ms feels smooth.
class ChatViewModel(private val repo: ChatRepo) : ViewModel() {
    private val _text = MutableStateFlow("")
    val text: StateFlow<String> = _text
    fun ask(q: String) = viewModelScope.launch {
        val sb = StringBuilder()
        repo.chatFlow(q)
            .onEach { sb.append(it) }
            .sample(40)                       // update UI at most every 40 ms
            .onCompletion { _text.value = sb.toString() }  // flush last text
            .catch { _text.value = sb.toString() + "\n[error]" }
            .collect { _text.value = sb.toString() }
    }
}
# Same idea in Python: accumulate chunks, render at most every 40 ms.
import time
buf, last = [], 0.0
async for t in tokens(q):
    buf.append(t)
    if time.monotonic() - last > 0.04:
        render("".join(buf)); last = time.monotonic()
render("".join(buf))
// Java/LiveData: accumulate in a StringBuilder, post at most every 40 ms.
long now = SystemClock.uptimeMillis();
sb.append(data);
if (now - last > 40) { text.postValue(sb.toString()); last = now; }

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Process death mid-stream? → Persist partial text and request id; on restart show partial text and offer retry or resume.
  • User scrolled up. → Autoscroll only when already at the bottom.
  • Markdown rendering cost? → Render incrementally and avoid re-parsing the whole text every update.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: moving state to the ViewModel and batching at 40 ms cut recompositions by about 20x and removed duplicate paid requests.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests only a background thread.
  • Hire: finds the ViewModel, scope and per-token update problems.
  • Strong hire: also fixes cancellation with awaitClose, lifecycle-aware collection, scroll behaviour and process death.

questions.contextHtml: To support offline mode you bundled a 2 GB 4-bit quantized Gemma model file in assets/ and run it with MediaPipe LLM Inference. After release: install conversion dropped 18%, crash-free sessions fell from 99.4% to 96.8%, and Crashlytics shows ANRs in generateResponse plus OutOfMemoryError on 3 GB RAM phones. Some users say the phone gets hot after five minutes, and the first answer takes 14 s on mid-range devices. A product manager wants a 50-message conversation window.
questions.promptHtml: What went wrong, and how do you redesign it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use a smaller model" without addressing delivery, threading, lifecycle and device gating.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Which devices and RAM tiers are affected? Do we need an open model or could Gemini Nano via AICore do the task? What tasks must work offline? Can the model be downloaded after install?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remotely disable the on-device path via a feature flag for low-RAM devices and fall back to the cloud or a message; ship a hotfix that moves inference off the main thread.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) 2 GB asset in the APK hurts install size and conversion; (b) inference or engine creation on the main thread causes ANRs; (c) the engine loaded repeatedly or two instances alive causes OOM; (d) a 2 GB model on 3 GB devices leaves too little RAM; (e) heavy sustained decoding causes heat and throttling.
  4. How I'd verify each: Play Console size and install metrics; StrictMode and ANR traces; heap dumps and LeakCanary; Android Profiler memory; a device lab across RAM tiers; thermal status API (PowerManager) logging.
  5. Root cause: Bundling the model, wrong thread, no lifecycle management of the engine, and no device capability gating.
  6. Fix: Download the model after install (Play Asset Delivery, Firebase ML model downloader or CDN) with a checksum, on Wi-Fi and charging constraints; create the engine once in a singleton, on a background dispatcher, close it when idle; gate by RAM class and a benchmark on first use; cap output tokens and context; check Gemini Nano first and use MediaPipe only where it is unavailable.
  7. Prevention: Device-tier tests, a size budget in CI, memory and thermal telemetry, staged rollout with feature flags.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not promise a 50-message window on a small model (context and memory cost); keep a short window plus a summary. I would not run long generations in the background.
# Local analogue: load once, reuse, small context.
from llama_cpp import Llama
llm = Llama(model_path="gemma-2b-it-q4.gguf", n_ctx=2048)   # verify path/flags
out = llm("Q: What is Kotlin?\nA:", max_tokens=64)
object LocalLlm {
    @Volatile private var llm: LlmInference? = null
    suspend fun get(context: Context, path: String): LlmInference =
        llm ?: withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
            LlmInference.createFromOptions(context,
                LlmInference.LlmInferenceOptions.builder()
                    .setModelPath(path).setMaxTokens(512).build()  // verify option names
            ).also { llm = it }
        }
    fun close() { llm?.close(); llm = null }
}
// Create once off the main thread, reuse, close when done (verify option names in docs).
LlmInference llm = LlmInference.createFromOptions(context,
    LlmInference.LlmInferenceOptions.builder().setModelPath(path).setMaxTokens(512).build());
String answer = llm.generateResponse("Explain coroutines in one sentence.");

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Quantization hurts quality. → Quantization stores weights with fewer bits (4-bit instead of 16-bit floats) to cut size and memory at some quality cost; evaluate on your tasks.
  • Model update strategy? → Versioned downloads with checksum and rollback.
  • Would you pick a smaller model? → Possibly, after measuring quality on the actual task.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a team shipped the model in assets, saw install rates fall, and recovered by moving to an opt-in post-install download with a size and battery prompt.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks a smaller model only.
  • Hire: moves download out of the APK, fixes threading and engine lifecycle, gates by device.
  • Strong hire: adds telemetry, thermal awareness, Gemini Nano first, context limits and staged rollout.

questions.contextHtml: A health-journal app (500k users) wants an "AI reflection" feature. Entries contain sensitive health notes. Requirements: works on a plane, p95 time to first token under 3 s, no sensitive text leaving the phone without consent, cloud budget of $4,000 per month, and legal wants the Play Data safety form to be accurate. Estimated usage: 60,000 reflections a day; the cloud model averages 900 input and 250 output tokens per call at 3 per million input and 15 per million output (example prices, verify). About 35% of devices support Gemini Nano.
questions.promptHtml: Design the routing and estimate the cloud cost.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Send everything to the cloud over HTTPS" or "do everything on-device", with no routing policy and no numbers.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: What does "sensitive" cover (all entries or tagged ones)? Is consent per-entry or global? Acceptable quality for the on-device path? Are summaries stored on the server?
  2. Immediate mitigation: (design problem) Start with the safest default: on-device only until consent is recorded.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) most requests can be served on-device for supported devices; (b) the cloud only for opted-in users or non-sensitive entries; (c) cache reduces repeats.
  4. How I'd verify each: Cost per call = (900 x 3 + 250 x 15) / 1,000,000 = 0.00645; for 60,000 calls a day that is 387 per day, about 11,600 per month, which is far above the $4,000 budget if everything goes to the cloud. If 35% use on-device and 30% of the rest are non-sensitive or opted out: cloud share is about 65% x 70% = 45%, so about 5,300 per month; still over budget, so add prompt caching, a cheaper model tier for simple reflections and output caps.
  5. Root cause of the tension: Quality, privacy and cost pull in different directions; routing resolves them.
  6. Fix: A router in the app: sensitive and offline -> on-device (Gemini Nano if AVAILABLE, else a downloadable MediaPipe model or a non-AI fallback); opted-in and online -> proxy with a small model tier; redact identifiers before upload; per-user daily caps.
  7. Prevention: Consent stored and enforced server-side; audit logs of routing decisions (not content); evals comparing on-device and cloud quality; accurate Data safety declarations.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: I would not silently upload entries "to improve quality". I would not compare quality by feel; use a fixed eval set. Some users on unsupported devices get a reduced feature; I state that clearly.
def route(entry, consent, online, nano_ok):
    if not consent or entry.sensitive:
        return "device" if nano_ok else "none"
    return "cloud" if online else ("device" if nano_ok else "none")
fun route(e: Entry, consent: Boolean, online: Boolean, nanoOk: Boolean): Route = when {
    !consent || e.sensitive -> if (nanoOk) Route.DEVICE else Route.NONE
    online -> Route.CLOUD
    else -> if (nanoOk) Route.DEVICE else Route.NONE
}
Route route(Entry e, boolean consent, boolean online, boolean nanoOk) {
    if (!consent || e.sensitive) return nanoOk ? Route.DEVICE : Route.NONE;
    if (online) return Route.CLOUD;
    return nanoOk ? Route.DEVICE : Route.NONE;
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Budget is cut to $2,000. → Cheaper tier model, shorter output cap, stronger caching, and a free-tier daily limit.
  • A regulator asks where data goes. → Show the routing map, retention terms and the consent records.
  • On-device quality is poor. → Narrow the task, improve the prompt, or offer cloud only after explicit consent.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: a sensitivity-aware router let a team ship a privacy-friendly feature at about half the projected cloud spend, mainly because consent defaults sent most entries on-device.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: all cloud or all device, no numbers.
  • Hire: routing by sensitivity, consent and availability with correct token arithmetic.
  • Strong hire: adds redaction, caching and tiering, server-side consent enforcement, audit logs, evals and honest limits for unsupported devices.

questions.contextHtml: After a viral week, daily active users doubled (40k to 80k) but your provider bill went from $210 to $1,450 a day. Metrics: average turns per conversation rose from 4 to 14; average input tokens per call rose from 900 to 5,200; output stayed around 250 tokens; the system prompt is 1,800 tokens and identical for every call; 30% of questions are repeat FAQs ("how do I reset my password?"). The latest app version also retries failed requests up to 5 times with no delay.
questions.promptHtml: Find where the money goes and cut cost by at least half without hurting quality.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Switch to a cheaper model for everything", which risks quality and ignores the structural causes.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Is there a usage field logged per call? What is the cache hit pattern? Do users need full-history recall? What quality metrics do we have?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap max_tokens server-side, add a per-user daily token quota, and cap retries to 2 with exponential backoff and jitter.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: (a) full history resent every turn (input grew about 5.8x); (b) the 1,800-token system prompt is paid on every call without caching; (c) repeated FAQs hit the model every time; (d) retry storms duplicate paid calls during provider 429s or timeouts; (e) all traffic uses the expensive tier.
  4. How I'd verify each: Token histograms by turn index from logged usage; ratio of duplicate prompts by normalised hash; retry counts per request id; provider dashboard split by model.
  5. Root cause: Input tokens dominate: per call 5,200 input vs 250 output. With example prices 3 and 15 per million, one call costs (5200 x 3 + 250 x 15)/1e6 = 0.0194; the 900-token version was 0.0065. Tripled cost per call times doubled users matches the bill.
  6. Fix: Summarise older turns and send summary plus the last 4 turns (target about 2,000 input tokens); enable provider prompt caching for the stable system prompt prefix (keep it first); serve FAQ answers from a response cache keyed by normalised question (30% fewer calls); route classification and short replies to a cheaper tier; stop retry storms.
  7. Prevention: Cost per active user dashboard, budget alerts, a token budget test in CI for the prompt builder, and per-feature quotas.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Summaries can lose details; I would keep key facts pinned and evaluate on a replay set. I would not cut history blindly at N turns without testing; and a response cache needs invalidation when answers change.
def build_messages(history, summary, keep_last=4):
    return ([{"role": "user", "content": f"Summary so far: {summary}"}]
            + history[-keep_last:])
fun buildMessages(history: List<Msg>, summary: String, keepLast: Int = 4): List<Msg> =
    listOf(Msg("user", "Summary so far: $summary")) + history.takeLast(keepLast)
List<Msg> buildMessages(List<Msg> history, String summary, int keepLast) {
    List<Msg> out = new ArrayList<>();
    out.add(new Msg("user", "Summary so far: " + summary));
    out.addAll(history.subList(Math.max(0, history.size() - keepLast), history.size()));
    return out;
}

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Quality drops after trimming. → Replay a fixed conversation set, compare, and adjust the window or summary prompt.
  • Prices change. → Keep prices in config, not code, and verify before each budget review.
  • Does caching hurt freshness? → Use a TTL and bust entries when source content changes.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A composite: history trimming plus FAQ caching cut input tokens by about 60%, and a retry cap removed a duplicate-spend bug nobody had noticed.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: only model downgrade.
  • Hire: identifies history growth, caching and retries, with token arithmetic.
  • Strong hire: quantifies the savings, adds guardrails (quotas, alerts), evaluates quality before and after, and lists trade-offs.

questions.subtopic: Cancelling upstream calls and failure modes
questions.promptHtml: What happens when a mobile client disconnects in the middle of a streamed LLM answer, and how do you make sure you neither waste money nor lose correctness?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Cancellation across three hops (app, proxy, provider) is where subtle cost and correctness bugs live. It separates people who have run streaming at scale.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: If nothing cancels the upstream call, the provider keeps generating and billing tokens nobody reads. The app cancels its SSE source, the proxy must notice the closed connection and cancel the provider stream, and I record the partial usage. For correctness I decide in advance whether a dropped answer is retried from scratch or resumed, and I make non-idempotent actions safe with request ids.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Chain of cancellation:

app: source.cancel()  ->  proxy: connection closed event  ->  provider stream: close/abort
  • In the app, awaitClose { es.cancel() } ties the call to the collector lifecycle.
  • In Spring WebFlux, cancelling the subscriber on the Flux propagates cancellation upstream if the provider client supports it; with servlet SSE, handle SseEmitter.onCompletion/onTimeout/onError and close the provider stream there.
  • In FastAPI, a disconnected client ends the generator; closing the with client.messages.stream(...) context aborts the upstream request.
  • Accounting: tokens generated before cancellation are usually billed; log partial usage and mark the request as cancelled.
  • Mobile reality: tunnels, backgrounding and screen-off kill connections constantly. Offer retry from the start (simple) or resume using a request id and the last event id (more work: the server must buffer recent chunks briefly).
  • Idempotency: if the model call triggers a side effect (tool call, email), tie it to a request id so retries do not repeat it.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
from fastapi import Request
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

@app.post("/api/chat/stream")
async def stream(body: dict, request: Request):
    async def gen():
        async with async_client.messages.stream(model="claude-sonnet-5-5", max_tokens=500,
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": body["question"]}]) as s:
            async for text in s.text_stream:
                if await request.is_disconnected():   # leaving the with-block aborts upstream
                    break
                yield f"data: {text}\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")
// Spring WebFlux: cancelling the subscriber cancels the upstream Flux; log it for accounting.
@PostMapping("/chat/stream", produces = [MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE])
fun stream(@RequestBody req: AskRequest): Flux<String> =
    chat.prompt().user(req.question).stream().content()
        .doOnCancel { log.info("client cancelled; closing upstream") }
@PostMapping(value = "/chat/stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
Flux<String> stream(@RequestBody Map<String, String> req) {
    return chat.prompt().user(req.get("question")).stream().content()
        .doOnCancel(() -> log.info("client cancelled; closing upstream"));
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Assuming a closed client connection automatically stops the provider call.
  • Retrying a half-finished stream and showing duplicated text.
  • Not logging cancelled requests, so the bill and the logs disagree.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Resume or restart? → Restart is simple and costs full tokens again; resume needs a server-side buffer keyed by request id and last event id, worth it only for long answers.
  2. How do you test it? → MockWebServer that drops the connection mid-stream plus a fake provider that records whether it was closed.
  3. What about tool calls mid-stream? → Execute side effects only after the model finishes the call, with idempotency keys.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: 3 YOE: "cancel the request when the user leaves". Senior: traces cancellation through all three hops, accounts for partial usage, chooses restart versus resume with reasons, and keeps side effects idempotent.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A proxy that never closed the provider stream on disconnect paid for full 1,000-token answers for users who had already left, a few percent of the daily bill until the cancellation hook was added.
